'''Maltese Sign Language''' ({{langx|mt|Lingwa tas-Sinjali Maltija}}, '''LSM''') is a young [[sign language]] of [[Malta]].<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RyVTDwAAQBAJ |title = The languages of Malta|isbn = 9783961100705|last1 = Gatt|first1 = Albert|year = 2018}}</ref>

==Development==
Maltese Sign Language has existed in some form since the 1950s, when education of deaf children officially started in 1956; however, signing was neither taught nor encouraged.<ref name="parallel">{{Cite book |last=Azzopardi-Alexander |first=Marie |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_languages_of_Malta/RyVTDwAAQBAJ|title=The languages of Malta |date=2018 |publisher=Language Science Press |isbn=978-3-96110-070-5 |editor-last=Gatt |editor-first=Albert |language=en |chapter=Maltese Sign Language: Parallel interwoven journeys of the Deaf community and the researchers}}</ref>{{rp|page=273}}<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=Pace |first=Simonne |date=2018-09-24 |title=Education of deaf children 'still poor' |url=https://timesofmalta.com/article/education-of-deaf-children-still-poor.689795 |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Times of Malta |language=en-gb}}</ref> LSM developed into its modern form in the 1980s, with the establishment of the first deaf club in Malta in 1981, at [[Lastaris Wharf]] in [[Valletta]].{{r|parallel|page=278}} This space allowed Deaf individuals to congregate and interact more regularly, allowing the language to proliferate and develop from more basic [[home sign]]s.{{r|parallel|page=278, 280}} The term "Maltese Sign Language" was first used in 1986.{{r|parallel|page=276}}

In the 1990s, signing began to be encouraged among Deaf students in some schools.{{r|parallel|page=275}} During early education involving sign language, teachers exposed students to signs from [[British Sign Language]] and [[Gestuno]]; however, these signs were largely not retained.{{r|parallel|page=276}}

Maltese Sign Language uses a one-handed alphabet system, unlike BSL, which has a two-handed alphabet. It is thought this system developed from 17th-century [[Spanish Sign Language]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Zammit |first=Juliana |date=2025-01-07 |title=The lesser known third official language of Malta |url=https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/133026/the_lesser_known_third_official_language_of_malta |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=[[Malta Today]] |language=en}}</ref>

== Official recognition and use ==
The [[Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Malta|Archdiocese of Malta]] has offered limited LSM interpretation of [[Mass in the Catholic Church|Mass]] since 2010. The Archdiocese has also translated scripture passages and some prayers into LSM, making these filmed translations available online.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2011-02-01 |title=A Welcoming Church for deaf persons in Malta |url=https://www.independent.com.mt/articles/2011-02-02/opinions/a-welcoming-church-for-deaf-persons-in-malta-287096/cookie-declaration |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=[[Malta Independent]]}}</ref>

LSM courses have been offered by the [[University of Malta]] since 2015.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Pace |first=Yannick |date=2021-11-24 |title=Malta's First Ever Crop Of Maltese Sign Language Interpreters Graduate From University |url=https://lovinmalta.com/news/maltas-first-ever-crop-of-maltese-sign-language-interpreters-graduate-from-university/ |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Lovin Malta |language=en-GB}}</ref>

In March 2016, the Maltese Parliament recognized LSM as an official language of the country.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Borg |first=Martina |date=2016-03-17 |title=Parliament gives Maltese sign language official recognition |url=https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/63266/parliament_gives_maltese_sign_language_official_recognition |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=MaltaToday.com.mt |language=en}}</ref> Following recognition of LSM nationally, the Maltese Sign Language Council was established "to advise on matters related to sign language, support research, and promote its development".<ref name=":0" />

Despite official recognition, the Deaf community in Malta has struggled with shortages of qualified LSM interpreters.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=de Jong |first=Belle |date=2021-07-25 |title=Concerns About Lack Of Maltese Sign Language Interpreter At COVID-19 Press Conferences Fall On Deaf Ears |url=https://lovinmalta.com/lifestyle/living-in-malta/concerns-about-lack-of-maltese-sign-language-interpreter-at-covid-19-press-conferences-fall-on-deaf-ears/ |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Lovin Malta |language=en-GB}}</ref> In 2000, the country had one interpreter; by 2014, only four, while there were 15 deaf students in Malta's schools who could benefit from interpretation.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Orland |first=Kevin Schembri |date=2014-11-15 |title=Lack of sign-language interpreters a problem for deaf community |url=https://www.independent.com.mt/articles/2014-11-15/local-interviews/Lack-of-sign-language-interpreters-a-problem-for-deaf-community-6736125673 |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=[[Malta Independent]]}}</ref> In 2016, Aġenzija Sapport launched an LSM interpretation service.<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2016-03-14 |title=Sign Language Interpreting Service launched |url=https://gozo.news/61304/sign-language-interpreting-service-launched/ |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Gozo News |language=en}}</ref> By 2018, the country had eight interpreters, five of whom worked for Aġenzija Sapport, and three who were freelancers.<ref name=":2" /> In October 2018, the University of Malta launched an LSM Interpretation postgraduate program;<ref name=":3" /> in November 2021, the University graduated its first class of LSM interpreters.<ref name=":1" />

== Vocabulary ==
Due to the young age of LSM in comparison to other sign languages, many signs are not fully standardized.<ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Azzopardi-Alexander |first=Marie |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Maltese_Linguistics/Zy4ykxfU78YC?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=%22Maltese+Sign+Language%22&pg=PA93&printsec=frontcover |title=Maltese Linguistics: A Snapshot; in Memory of Joseph A. Cremona (1922 - 2003) |date=2009 |publisher=Brockmeyer Verlag |isbn=978-3-8196-0734-9 |editor-last=Fabri |editor-first=Ray |pages=93–116 |language=en |chapter=Iconicity and the development of Maltese Sign Language}}</ref> LSM speakers both develop their own signs and adopt signs from other sign languages when a standardized sign does not exist.<ref name=":4" /> Some adopted signs are maintained in their original form, while others are adapted into a form unique to LSM.<ref name=":4" />

As with other sign languages, LSM makes use of many iconic signs, ie, signs that reference the specific traits or features of the idea being described. For example, the sign for book uses both hands to mimic opening a book. These more basic iconic signs tend to develop into more arbitrary signs for related concepts; the sign for library uses a similar motion to the sign for book, but with a different hand shape.<ref name=":4" />

Many signs referring to locations draw on specific geographic or social traits; for example, the sign for house references the flat roofs of Maltese houses, while the sign for the island of [[Gozo]] references its three hills.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":4" />

When forming new signs to describe more specific subjects, signers often sign the general term followed by a more specific descriptor; for example, the sign for "dog" followed by "spots" creates the sign "[[Dalmatian dog|Dalmatian]]".<ref name=":4" />

The LSM [[Fingerspelling|manual alphabet]] is used in combination with other signs. One such combination is a sign for [[Mediterranean Sea|Mediterranean]] ("Mediterran" in Maltese), which combines the letter handshape "M" with the sign for "sea".<ref name=":4" /> Some place names use fingerspelled abbreviations of Maltese names, such as "ATT" for [[Attard]].<ref name=":4" />

Younger signers tend to use the LSM manual alphabet more frequently than older signers, potentially due to lower literacy rates among the older population.<ref name=":4" />

==Academic study and recording==
LSM began to be studied by academics in the 1994.{{r|parallel|page=282}}<ref name=":4" /> The Maltese Sign Language Research Project was set up at the [[University of Malta]], and published two volumes of a sign language dictionary in 2003 and 2004.{{r|parallel|page=282}}

Maria Galea has described the use of [[SignWriting]] when used to write Maltese Sign Language.<ref name="GaleaLinguistic">{{cite book
|last=Galea
|first=Maria
|title=SignWriting (SW) of Maltese Sign Language (LSM) and its development into an orthography: Linguistic considerations
|year=2014
|type=Ph.D. dissertation
|publisher=University of Malta
|location=Malta
|url=https://www.academia.edu/10451785
|access-date=2015-02-04}}</ref>

In the late 2010s, academics began work on an online, filmed LSM dictionary.<ref name=":2" />

==In media==
The Maltese [[Public broadcasting|public broadcaster]] [[Public Broadcasting Services|PBS Ltd.]] began airing a nightly newscast in LSM on its [[TVM2]] network in 2012.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Vella|first1=Matthew|title=PBS takes Education 22 in cultural revamp of station|url=http://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/16556/pbs-takes-education-22-in-cultural-revamp-of-station-20120305|access-date=2016-02-23|work=MaltaToday|date=2012-03-05}}</ref>

LSM interpretation has been broadcast alongside episodes of ''[[Peppa Pig]]'' in Malta since January 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Galea |first=Charlene |date=2025-01-28 |title=Watch: Peppa Pig Bil-Malti Goes Inclusive With English Subtitles And Maltese Sign Language |url=https://lovinmalta.com/news/watch-peppa-pig-bil-malti-goes-inclusive-with-english-subtitles-and-maltese-sign-language/ |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Lovin Malta |language=en-GB}}</ref>
